quote: Oh, you claim to conceive it, but you never believe it. As Wittgenstein said, “If there were a verb meaning ‘to believe falsely,’ it would not have any significant first person, present indicative.”
content: Wittgenstein is cast as the postmodernist here and he is on the other side. The remark (Philosophical Investigations, Part II §x) is his gloss on Moore’s paradox, the oddity of asserting “it is raining and I don’t believe it is raining,” and his point is that the first-person present “I believe” functions as an assertion of the content rather than as a report of a mental state, which is why “I falsely believe p” cannot be sincerely said. That is a thesis about the pragmatics of assertion, and it is fully compatible with, indeed presupposes, the distinction between belief and truth that the essay is defending: the paradox arises because “p” and “I believe p” have different truth conditions while having the same assertoric force. The standard modern treatments (Shoemaker’s “Moore’s Paradox and Self-Knowledge,” 1995; Heal (1994)) take this as the starting point. Nobody in the relativist tradition the essay is parodying has, as far as I can find, cited this passage for the claim that belief and truth are the same; the quotation has been put in the wrong mouth to make the dialogue go.

quote: To make a long story short, it turns out that there’s a very natural way of scoring the accuracy of a probability assignment, as compared to reality: just take the logarithm of the probability assigned to the real state of affairs.
content: The log score is one of a family of proper scoring rules (Brier’s quadratic score from 1950, the spherical score, and the continuum characterized by Gneiting & Raftery (2007)), and the choice among them is a choice, with consequences. The log score is the unique local proper score (Bernardo (1979)), which is a good reason to prefer it, but it is also unbounded: an agent who assigns probability zero to what happens scores negative infinity, and the ordering of two agents’ accuracy can reverse between log and Brier scoring on the same forecasts. The essay says the score is “very natural” and leaves it there, and then builds on it the claim that a probability assignment “cannot possibly be true,” only accurate. That second claim is odd given what the scoring-rule literature is for: Joyce’s accuracy argument for probabilism (Joyce (1998)) treats a credence function as an estimate of the truth-values and scores it by its distance from them, so “closeness to truth” is the primitive and the essay’s type error is the field’s foundation. There is no contradiction, but there is no discovery either; the essay has renamed truth-likeness “accuracy” and declared the original word a category mistake.

quote: All this should not be confused with the statement “I assign 70% credence that ‘snow is white.’ ” I may well believe that proposition with probability ∼1— be quite certain that this is in fact my belief.
content: The parenthetical concession later (“beliefs about beliefs are not always accurate”) understates how badly this assumption does empirically. Stated probabilities are constructed at the moment of elicitation and move with the format of the question: numerical and verbal elicitations of the same person’s uncertainty disagree (Windschitl & Wells (1996)), the same credence elicited as a probability, as odds, or as a betting price comes out different, and the confidence–accuracy literature shows that people’s reports of how sure they are track accuracy weakly and are distorted by ease of processing. Nisbett and Wilson’s finding, discussed in Book II, that people confabulate the causes of their own judgments extends to the judgments themselves. So the essay’s picture, on which credences about the world are uncertain but one’s credences about one’s own credences are “∼1,” has the confidence in the wrong place: the one number in the essay that a reader can be fairly sure is not exactly right is the 70%, because there is no stable fact about the reader’s credence for it to be right about. The type distinction the essay draws is sound; the assumption that the inner term is known with near-certainty is what makes the arithmetic that follows look cleaner than the psychology allows.
